News.title: Murder probe launched after pedestrian, 26, dies in ‘hit-and-run’ – as five people are arrested
News.content:
HORROR CRASH Murder probe launched after pedestrian, 26, dies in ‘hit-and-run’ – as five people are arrested

A MURDER investigation has been launched after a reported hit-and-run left a pedestrian dead – with five people arrested.

A 26-year-old man was rushed to hospital with life-threatening injuries and despite the best efforts of medical staff sadly died.



Police received reports of a collision involving a car and a pedestrian at just after 8.30pm last night in Doncaster.

A silver Hyundai is understood to have been involved and reportedly failed to stop at the scene in Prince’s Street.



Officers arrested a 30-year-old and a 22-year-old man on suspicion of murder.

A 20-year-old man, a 38-year-old woman and a 24-year-old woman have been arrested on suspicion of assisting offenders.

They all remain in police custody at this time.

Prince’s Road was closed whilst officers were at the scene and has since reopened.

If you have any information that could help with our investigation, please get in touch via our Public Portal.

You can submit dashcam footage here.

You can provide information anonymously via independent charity Crimestoppers at https://crimestoppers-uk.org/.

News.title: How chance photo of a badly parked car unlocked sickening case  of mum-of-five stabbed 11 times in a field
News.content:
GRUESOME PLOT How chance photo of a badly parked car unlocked sickening case of mum-of-five stabbed 11 times in a field

WHEN mum-of-five Pennie Davis made her daily trip to tend to her horse, in 2014, she had no idea the danger she was in.

Hours later the 47-year-old mother-of-five was found dead in the field, close to her home in the idyllic New Forest, by devastated husband Pete. She had been stabbed 11 times.





Initially cops had little to go on, other than a car key found next to her body, but there was no car and no known motive for this brutal attack in broad daylight.

The remote location meant there was very little chance of any witnesses to Pennie’s murder – no CCTV and no house-to-house enquiries to be done.

Det Supt Paul Barton says: “This was a frenzied, vicious, personal attack against Pennie, so we were looking for someone who is extremely dangerous.”

Now criminologist and investigative journalist Donal McIntyre’s new documentary reveals how a local man’s photo of a badly parked car was to help police unlock the investigation and untangle a murderous plot that cost Pennie her life.

It was early evening on 2 September, 2014, when a distraught man called 999 saying he had just found his wife’s body next to one of her horses in a remote paddock.

At first police didn’t know if Pennie had fallen from her horse, or if the horse had reared and trampled her in a freak accident.

But a post-mortem examination revealed Pennie had been murdered – stabbed to death.



Police had to focus on their only clue – the car key found next to Pennie’s body.

It didn’t belong to Pennie’s husband Pete who had found her body. His alibi checked out and he was quickly ruled out as a suspect.

So now the family liaison officers were tasked with delving into Pennie’s personal life to find out any reason why somebody might want her dead.



Pennie had been married before and, when it ended in 2012, it left bad blood between the families.

She had accused her stepson Ben Carr of sexual assault against two children, creating tensions – but officers did not think this was relevant to Pennie’s murder.

Meanwhile local man Tony Norris came forward to say he had seen a silver Vauxhall Zafira parked up on a bridge near to where Pennie’s body had been found. He thought it was unusual so he took a picture of the registration number.

He had also seen a man and a woman trying the doors of the vehicle, before a low-loader came to take the car away.

The woman who owned the car told police she had lent it to a man called Justin Robertson. He had lost the car key and had to get a tow truck to pick the car up.



Police tried the key they had found next to Pennie’s body and it discovered it belonged to the same car.

Justin Robertson was now a key suspect in Pennie’s murder – but he was missing.

His mobile phone data revealed a number which kept popping up in the two weeks before Pennie’s death – but all communication between them stopped as soon as Pennie’s body was found.



And that number belonged to Pennie’s stepson Ben Carr.

Donal McIntyre says: “It was a major breakthrough. And Carr is the crucial link between Robertson, who dropped the key at the crime scene, and Pennie. But Robertson is nowhere to be found – he is dangerous and on the run.”

Police knew that Robertson was a low-level drug dealer and that Ben Carr used drugs.

But the level of regular conversations between the two, that stopped as soon as Pennie died, and the fact that there was bad blood between Carr and Pennie seemed more than coincidence.



Carr was brought in for questioning but had an alibi for the time of Pennie’s murder and police had no choice but to release him on bail.

Detectives then turned to Pennie’s social media to look for any stronger motive for her murder.

Paul Barton says: “About two weeks before her death she had what I would describe as a bit of a drunken rant on Facebook messenger with a female regarding this female’s upcoming marriage to Ben Carr’s father.

“This rant from Pennie was essentially telling this female does she know what she is getting herself into with this family?

“That Ben Carr is a nasty piece of work and he is alleged to have assaulted two females in the past and that she is going resurrect this and get him arrested on their wedding day and cause as much embarrassment and disruption on the day.



“So this was starting to build up a strong picture of Ben Carr wanting Pennie silenced and perhaps he has used Justin Robertson to do that.”

With Robertson still on the run, police looked for further evidence that he went to the field that day to confront Pennie.

CCTV footage from the Montague Arms in Beaulieu showed Pennie’s car being followed by a silver Vauxhall Zafira.

Paul Barton says: “We couldn’t say Robertson was the driver at that time but we knew Robertson had access to that vehicle.

“More importantly we were able to go back 24 hours and see Pennie doing the same journey and more worryingly, the Zafira following her the day before.



“This shows that this was premeditated and she was effectively being targeted.”

Robertson’s mobile phone data revealed he had been carrying out the same journey as Pennie on the day of her murder.

Then Robertson’s girlfriend Leanne Doyle revealed he had visited her on the day of the murder and had a kitchen knife in his possession.

“He said something like ‘you want to watch the news tonight. Something big has happened’,” says Paul Barton.

Doyle appeared to know nothing about the murder, but when she was arrested she revealed that Robertson had turned up at her address with a pair of trainers and asked her to dispose of them for him.



She was charged with assisting an offender. With Robertson still on the run, more and more circumstantial evidence was pointing to him being the murderer.

Robertson had ditched the phone which could have revealed his location, meaning the police were still one step behind him.

But a week after Pennie’s murder he turned himself in.



Paul Barton says: “To my amazement he actually spoke to officers, in fact we couldn’t stop him talking. He was confident.

“He had had a week to rehearse what he was going to say. He was basically saying that he wasn’t responsible for Pennie’s death, he didn’t know her and that he is not that sort of person.

“He is more of a thief and a burglar but he certainly doesn’t go round killing people.”

During the interview, police started to put the evidence to him, including the Zafira and the car key.

Paul Barton says: “He had to think quickly and he said he was out in that area looking for houses to burgle and he lost the key somewhere.



“It may have been in that field and if it was I certainly didn’t see anybody in that field.”

Police then decided to re-arrest Pennie’s stepson Ben Carr.

Officers searched his property and found a roll of banknotes totalling £1,500 which turned out to be counterfeit. Detectives believed Carr was planning to use this money to pay Robertson for killing Pennie.

Both men were charged with conspiracy to murder and Robertson was also facing a murder charge.

Carr’s lawyers decided he would give evidence and submitted his defence statement.



Paul Barton says: “What Carr submitted was a surprise to us.

“He was potentially going to be accused of assaulting two girls and potentially be arrested on his father’s wedding day, so the only way he could stop that was silencing Pennie.

“In fact he was going to pay Robertson £1,500 to go and scare Pennie to stop her making these threats.

“So he was now admitting there was a link between the two of them. He is saying Robertson has had contact with Pennie Davis and we didn’t have any forensic evidence to suggest that was the case, it was circumstantial at that point.”

Carr’s partial admission made it even harder for Robertson to deny he was in the paddock that day.



Paul Barton says: “So Ben Carr’s version of events was that Robertson approached Pennie and he was wearing a balaclava and brandishing a knife.

“And that Pennie fought and ripped off the balaclava so saw his identification and as a result of that he had no option but to stab her 11 times and kill her.

“For me it reinforced what we thought had happened all along. The only difference was Ben Carr’s version of events that he didn’t want Pennie killed. We say that he did,”



The jury at Winchester Crown Court found Robertson guilty of murder and conspiracy to murder. He was jailed for life with a minimum term of 32 years.

Ben Carr was also found guilty of conspiracy to murder and jailed for life with a minimum term of 30 years.

At a later date Leanne Doyle was found guilty of perverting the course of justice and jailed for 10 months.

Paul Barton says: “For me the most critical piece of evidence was the car key that was found next to Pennie’s body because that linked to a vehicle which was being used by Justin Robertson.”

Donal McIntyre says: “Pennie Davis was a much-loved mother of five who had everything to live for.



“Her callous murderer left no forensic evidence at the scene but carelessly dropped a car key during the vicious attack.

“This kickstarted a highly complex and detailed investigation.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But the dogged determination of experienced detectives now means that two dangerous men will now spend the rest of their lives behind bars.”

Donal MacIntyre’s UK Killer Evidence S3 airs Mondays at 10 pm from 6 April on The TRUE CRIME channel.

News.title: How once-thriving town became UK’s unemployment capital as jobless benefits claimants proudly brag ‘working is for mugs’
News.content:
DOLE PATROL How once-thriving town became UK’s unemployment capital as jobless benefits claimants proudly brag ‘working is for mugs’

WHEN Sandra Craggs left school aged 16, there was no shortage of jobs on offer.

Such was the range of opportunities in Ebbw Vale 60 years ago, if she wasn’t happy in her place of work, she could – and often did – quit on a Friday and walk into new employment the following Monday.





The town in the heart of the Welsh Valleys was pumping out steel and its many factories were supplying goods around the globe.

“If you weren’t working there was something seriously wrong with you,” says Mrs Craggs, now 76.

When you tell her that her home town now tops the UK league for unemployment, she looks like she is about to burst into tears as she sits chatting and drinking tea with her friends at a local church.



“How’s it come to this?” she asks. “It is just too sad. Me and my friends all had jobs from the day we left school and none of us would ever have thought any different.

“We had the biggest steel industry in the world here and so many factories, making everything you can imagine. I spent many years working in a ladies’ underwear factory and I loved it.

“What hope is there for young people living here now?”

Not much, according to the latest data released by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) on working-age benefit combinations.



This looks at the total number of people aged 16 to 65 claiming either Universal Credit with no work requirement and/or Jobseeker’s Allowance.

In Blaenau Gwent, which includes the town of Ebbw Vale, almost 40 per cent of the working-age population is currently claiming support, meaning nearly two in every five residents aged 18 to 65 are on the books.

New figures show that, of the area’s 41,235 working-age residents, 15,772 are claiming benefits – including 6,773 on Universal Credit who are not required to seek work.

And 20 minutes up the road, the area of Merthyr Tydfil ranks third on the list, with a 36.2 per cent claim rate. In total, 12,873 residents receive monthly DWP payments, out of a working-age population of 35,602.

The figures come as it was revealed the number of “NEETs” – those not in education, employment, or training – has hit 957,000 in the UK, up 36,000 since Labour came to power.



In Wales, Labour has held power in the Senedd, formerly the National Assembly for Wales, continually since its inception in 1999.

All of which leaves Mrs Craggs shaking her head. “This town was absolutely buzzing when I was growing up. Everyone was in work and had money in their pocket,” she says.

“Nowadays the only money in most people’s pockets is from the benefits office.

“It’s not good for people, especially the young ones. They need jobs to give them self-respect and good self-esteem, like we had when we were young. It breaks my heart, it does.”



Her friends nod hard in agreement. One, 84-year-old Val Davies, says: “The benefits system has become a culture here. Kids are growing up in families where no one has ever worked.

“If you see your parents and grandparents living off benefits, you’re going to have the mindset from an early age that you’ll do the same.

“We need to break the cycle, somehow, and give people their pride back.



“The Government needs to step in and create an economic climate here that gives business leaders some hope. If they do that, the jobs will follow.”

Her friend, Jen Caswell, 78, experienced the decline in Ebbw Vale’s fortunes first hand towards the end of her working life. “I had 11 jobs in a row where the companies I worked for went out of business,” she explains.

“I’d always worked hard and I’d been in work since I left school.

“But in the 90s it started to go very wrong. The coal mines had all been closed down and the steelworks were coming to an end. The town was changing, and not for the better.

“But I still wanted to work and chased any job I could get, but every job I got ended because the company went bust.



“My last job was at the local police station, but even that got closed down while I was there. I was ready to retire by then anyway, but I was really upset at the time.

“I started wondering whether I was the jinx. Now I realise of course that those 11 jobs were the markers of what was happening here.

“It has turned this town into a shadow of what it used to be.”



In the town centre, boarded-up shops, a long-closed shopping centre and the sight of men drinking pints and smoking outside pubs in the middle of the day tell their own story.

Opposite the town’s Wetherspoons pub, once a cinema house, we find Ian, 50, who is homeless, lying under blankets in a doorway outside a public toilet. At least that is still open, he muses.

Ian has been in and out of jail all his life and has never held down a job. Now he wishes he was back in prison, he says, adding: “I get clean clothes and three hot meals every day when I’m inside.

“And a nice warm bed.”

With him is 35-year-old Mark, who says he is pulling in £250 a week on disability benefits and lives in a two-bed flat nearby, paid for by housing benefit.



He says he is unable to work due to a back injury but admits that even if he could work, he wouldn’t.

“Why the f*** would I work?” he says. “I get my flat paid for and £250 in my back pocket every week on the state.

“Working is for mugs. The few people I know who do work have no money to pay for their gas and electric because they’re not paid enough to pay all their bills and they’re always knackered.

“I don’t have to worry about any of that.

“I can fully understand why everyone around here is on benefits. It’s easy but I admit it has made us all incredibly lazy.



“I didn’t used to be lazy. I was in the Army and I gave it everything but then I got a medical discharge due to my back injury and that gave me access to every benefit going.

“They’d have to pay me a lot of money to get me back into work. I’d want three grand a week minimum.”

Not everyone in the town shares Mark’s distaste for paid employment. Alisha, 23, spent years studying for health and social care qualifications in order to pursue her dream of a career in the sector.



Alisha, who is a support worker for people with mental disabilities, says: “I worked super hard to have a job I wanted and a career that I feel is worth having.

“It is difficult to find work around here so you have to push really hard to make it happen.

“You have to find your niche and get the qualifications you need to be of value because that’s the only way into a job here.

“I admit some people in the town don’t work because they can’t be bothered. It’s easier to stay on Universal Credit for some people. That’s their choice, I guess.

“But I think the bigger problem is a lack of opportunity in the area. I know young people who want to work but there just aren’t jobs and when they find a vacancy, they’re told they don’t have enough experience.”



Teaching assistant Jack, 29, says he and his group of friends are all in work and that the jobs are there for people who want to find them.

He says: “Me and my friends are all in our late 20s and early 30s and we’ve all got jobs. I know there are plenty of jobs around here because I‘ve looked on employment websites.

“I think the problem is that a lot of people, especially the young ones – Gen Z and the like – just don’t want to work.



“They spend all their time online and think they should be working as influencers but that’s not proper work. When I was a teenager I was out riding my bike or playing in the park, not glued to a screen.

“Social media and the internet is making young people lazy and that worries me.”

From her shop window in the centre of town, Jo Curtis sees it all. Gangs of teenagers, many dressed from head to toe in black and many riding electric bikes, are terrorising Ebbw Vale, she says.

“They rob the elderly and behave as if they run the place. They’re little monsters. Sometimes there’s as many as 40 or even 50 of them swarming through the town. Some are as young as 11, but mostly they’re around 13 to 16 years old, I’d say.”

A few weeks ago, a group of them on their way to school stopped at the town’s Greggs store to raid it. “They grabbed anything they could – pies, sausage rolls, cans of fizzy drink – then legged it,” says Jo.



“They’ve also been using slingshots to fire stones at car windscreens as they drive around the town. There’s been a spate of these attacks in recent months.

“The cops put up dispersal orders in the town every few weeks to keep them out, but it doesn’t seem to make much difference from what I can see.

“Where are the kids’ parents? These youths are out on the streets until midnight when they ought to be at home.”



Jo opened her print shop in Ebbw Vale seven months ago and says the gangs of feral youths are making the town a “no-go” area for many. “It’s too dangerous at night. Most people stay indoors now.”

As for the town’s economy, Jo would like more government intervention to kickstart it.

She says: “There is a lot of poverty in the area, fuelled by unemployment and a lack of industry. We’re stuck in a vicious circle and currently the only solution on offer seems to be endless benefit payments, which make people lazy.

“I think that public money would be better spent creating job opportunities and more vocational training for kids when they’re in school.

“They also need to be taught how to manage money and general economics.”



A DWP source tells The Sun: “We are determined to break down barriers to opportunity and boost employment across the UK, including by transforming job centres, through our expanded Youth Guarantee and apprenticeship reforms, and by providing personalised work and skills support to those who need it.

“That is why we have given £20million to Wales to fund trailblazers tackling the unique challenges faced by communities including Blaenau Gwent, and there is also a Youth Hub in the area helping young people into training and work.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

At the town’s sprawling job centre on an industrial estate opposite a Tesco superstore, we count 50 staff – but not one job seeker.

“Making Work Pay” posters are emblazoned across almost every wall and window, but other than the civil servants who trudge in to the brown concrete building every day, no one is there to read them. Perhaps they’ve already worked out what pays.

News.title: Mystery as grandad, 65, shot dead and dumped in shallow grave after suddenly vanishing as heartbroken family pay tribute
News.content:
FOUL PLAY Mystery as grandad, 65, shot dead and dumped in shallow grave after suddenly vanishing as heartbroken family pay tribute

A GRANDAD has been found shot dead in a shallow grave on a farm after going missing for days – with his heartbroken family paying tribute.

Richard Wills, 65, vanished on Easter Sunday after leaving his home in Victoria, Australia, before being reported missing when he didn’t return for lunch.



The beloved grandad was last seen leaving his Hughs St home in Ouyen at about 8am last Sunday.



Richard’s family told cops he had gone to work on his rural property on the Mallee Highway – part of his normal routine.

But mysteriously he never returned, forcing them to alert police.

On Tuesday his body was found buried during a search of the property at about 1:30pm local time.

Local police said he had been fatally shot, before confirming he had died as a result of foul play.



Senior sergeant Steve Trewavas said: “Sadly, Richard has clearly met with foul play.

“What is still unclear is exactly who was involved, and why.”

He added: “We are very keen to speak to anyone who may have any knowledge of the circumstances which led to his death and who was responsible.

“We’re hoping that this appeal leads to someone coming forward and doing the right thing – it can be done anonymously – so that we can hold those responsible to account.”



The victim’s wife Donna said they have “lots of grandkids that are going to miss him”.

The heartbroken widow said: “If he saw someone stopped on the side of the road he’d be the one who would turn around, go back, and make sure they were alright.”

Police have appealed to anyone with information to come forward to help them with their investigation.

News.title: Woman, 19, dies after dog attack as animal seized & man, 37, arrested in Essex
News.content:
DOG HORROR Woman, 19, dies after dog attack as animal seized & man, 37, arrested in Essex

A 19-YEAR-old teenager has died following a dog attack at a home in Essex.

Police arrived at the property in Dunmow at 10:45pm on April 10.



A young woman was found by officers seriously injured at the premises.



Despite the efforts of emergency services, the teen was pronounced dead at the scene.

A 37-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of being in charge of a dog dangerously out of control and causing injury that led to death.

The man from Dunmow remains in custody.

Essex Police said it believed that the girl had been attacked by the dog at the property.

Specialist officers were called to the house in Leaden Roding to seize the dog and ensure the scene was safe.

Assistant Chief Constable Stuart Hooper said: “I know this incident will be a shock to the local community.

“My thoughts, and those of us all at Essex Police, are with the loved ones of the woman who died yesterday.

“We will have officers in the area throughout today so please come and speak to them if you have any information or have any concerns.



“Experienced detectives are leading the investigation to understand exactly what has happened.”

Coppers are asking for anyone with information, CCTV, or other footage of the incident to contact it using the quote incident 1419 of 10 April.
