News.title: Inside world’s ‘murder capital’ as city sees 2 killed daily with bodies littering streets… & why it’s about to get WORSE
News.content:
ONCE a postcard-perfect playground for sun-seeking tourists, the ‘world’s murder capital’ is anything but idyllic after its descent into bloody chaos.

Behind the black sand beaches and luxury resorts, the coastal city is now filled with the screams of innocent people as rival murder gangs wage a brutal war on the streets in their bid to seize territory. Here, The Sun takes a closer look at the horrors unfolding.



Journalists, students, Brits abroad and even federal judges have all been gunned down in crossfire or through suspected assassinations in the Mexican city of Colima.

And it means one of the country’s smallest states now holds the horrifying title of the world’s most deadly capital.



More than 620 brutal homicides were recorded last year – a huge number in a population of just 700,000 – with around two murders being committed every day.

The city is being carved up by the violent turf wars between the formidable Sinaloa Cartel, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), and Los Zetas.

Their brutal war has escalated in recent years as the bloodthirsty cartel groups look to expand control and has now turned the once bustling holiday hotspot that once saw 1.5million visitors a year into a warzone with locals and visitors all caught in the crossfire.

British software engineer Ben Corser, 37, was gunned down in 2022 while shopping at a supermarket with three pals in Colima City and is thought to have been a victim of the cartels.

His devastated family said he was “in the wrong place at the wrong time”.



A year later, 70 people were killed in one month, including a university student who played American football, a doctor from the State Institute of Oncology, and a 16-year-old boy.

Revenge attacks between the warring sides have also seen the discovery of bags containing decomposing body parts, bodies hanging in public and even severed heads being chucked down the street.

Now, experts warn the carnage is set to spike after the death of feared drug lord El Mencho sparked a tinderbox of violence across the country.

Power struggles between potential successors or defections are “likely to increase violence significantly”, Rafaella Lipschitz of New Lines Institute told The Sun.

El Mencho – leader of the CJNG – was killed during a special forces military operation in the western state of Jalisco, in February this year.



Retaliatory violence exploded across more than a dozen states, including bordering Colima, as cartel fighters unleashed a coordinated show of force that shut down streets and sent tourists fleeing.

Rafaella described the attacks, which saw 73 people slaughtered, including 25 Mexican National Guard, as “an expression of cartel power and an effort to reestablish deterrence against the government”.

British expats who once moved to the idyllic country, dreaming of a more luxurious life, suddenly found themselves at risk of being caught in the crossfire.

Simon Coulson, 53, originally from Nuneaton in Warwickshire, told The Sun: “We were being told that the cartels were going to run into people’s houses and start shooting.

“This is not something we want to live with on a regular basis.”



One of Simon’s darkest fears came alive as cartel terror ripped through his neighbourhood.

The 53-year-old described the destruction he encountered as he desperately tried to drive home from his mother-in-law’s through battle-torn streets.



He said: “There was ash, glass and bits of metal in the roads.

“So we had to drive around them – on a highway doing 60/70 miles an hour.”

Colima’s cartel chaos

The CJNG is one of Mexico’s most powerful and fastest-growing criminal organisations, with violence as its calling card.

The group launched itself on the national stage in 2011 by dumping 35 bodies under a bridge in the state of Veracruz.

And their presence has been well established in Colima.



Just last year, 54 suspected members were arrested by authorities in the state along with hoards of firearms, ammunition, knives and stolen vehicles.

But Colima was already a hotbed of cartel violence due to a key drug port in its town of Manzanillo, the main tourist spot in the state.

The Pacific port welcomes almost 3.5million cargo shipments a year – more than any other port in Mexico – and is perfectly positioned on the cartels’ usual smuggling routes.

Manzanillo serves as an arrival point for methamphetamine from Asia and a transit point for drugs moving towards the United States and Europe.

Just last month, the Mexican Navy seized a ‘narco-sub’ carrying nearly four tonnes of cocaine off Manzanillo’s coast.



As holidaymakers flock to the vacation spot, the ruthless trio of cartels vie for control over the key port and its riches.

Mexico Analyst at International Crisis Group, David Mora, told The Sun: “Manzanillo doesn’t just act as an entry point for cartel drugs; these groups are also shipping their illicit goods out from the port.



“Recently, they have started exporting illegal mercury, which has a significant market price.”

And daily reminders of the lengths the three gangs are willing to go to are left for all to see.

Mutilated bodies or brazen broad-daylight killings often serve as warnings to rival cartels to back away before things turn even nastier.

Ten years of a militarised campaign against the cartels has not ended the trade in drugs or helped enforce the rule of law.

Even snatching top drug lords cannot cripple a trade worth billions of dollars a year, as others emerge to take their place.



Government crackdowns have also splintered crime factions into vicious armed units, broadening an already bloody war.

David said: “We’re not just talking about three groups fighting each other anymore.

“The Sinaloa cartel has splintered into proxy cells, and other groups are diversifying.”

Cartels are also transitioning into “quasi-military” style warfare, David said.

He added: “The recent wave of attacks was overt but targeted. They hit government banks and blocked popular convenience stores.



“The killings and kidnappings have become more specific.”

The dramatic nature of cartel battles means there “will always be civilian casualties”, David said.

‘I saw body lying in the street’

But astonishingly, residents have adapted to the brutal war zone they call home.

David said: “I spoke with people in Colima last week, and they said they are very afraid.

“But that is not the rule. It is shocking to see how people adapt. They know the places and routes that are safe and avoid the danger.”



Colima was once the safest place to live in Mexico, with almost all locals having access to electricity, running water and a sewage system.

But the homicide rate has tripled since 2015, accompanied by a rise in public murders of high-profile political and social leaders.

Witnessing the murders in the street is just part of life.

“A young man was murdered about 100 metres from my house. They mistook him for someone selling drugs,” Joel Vargas told Al Jazeera in 2016.

“They also killed the owner of a car wash in my neighbourhood. I’d just left home when I heard the shots, and moments later I saw the body lying on the street, covered with a sheet.”



In 2022, tensions reached a boiling point as a mass street brawl between the CJNG and Sinaloa crew broke out.

Those involved in the senseless beatings were all put behind bars in the same prison, leading to chaos.

The incarceration didn’t stop the fighting, with ten inmates massacred and seven more injured as the two gangs battled behind bars.

During holy week a year later, ten people were murdered in Colima in just 48 hours.

The spate of crimes included a mutilated head being left on the street in Manzanillo, with a warning note from La Barredora, Sinaloa’s armed wing, telling the CJNG not to invade its territory.



Three of the senseless killings, including a 12-year-old girl, took place in the capital Colima, following on from six there, the previous week.

Raffaella said: “The threat of continued, or even elevated levels of violence, comes down to CJNG’s internal leadership dynamics now that El Mencho has been eliminated.

“If the group can agree on a single successor, things may continue ‘as normal.’

“But if we see a splintering, power struggles between different potential leaders, or defections of plaza bosses and lieutenants, violence is likely to increase significantly.”

News.title: Extraordinary £334million, 439ft superyacht with 2 pools arrives in UK before being handed over to Chinese billionaire
News.content:
FLOATING PALACE Extraordinary £334million, 439ft superyacht with 2 pools arrives in UK before being handed over to Chinese billionaire

A PALATIAL £334million superyacht has turned heads on the South coast before being handed over to its Chinese billionaire owner.

Deep Blue is a 439ft, 9,000-tonne, five-deck luxury yacht with its own helipad and two swimming pools.





The gargantuan vessel was designed and constructed by German luxury shipbuilders Lürssen.

It launched from Lemweder port in Germany on earlier in the week and stopped off in Dorset on the South coast of England yesterday.

Although the building of the yacht and its purchase has been incredibly secretive, it is believed to be owned by Chinese billionaire Richard Qiangdong Liu.

Liu is the founder of Chinese online retail behemoth JD.com, and he is worth an estimated £4billion.

He started out by opening an electrical goods shop in 1998 before founding JD.com in 2004.

Boaties at Poole Harbour on Friday were astonished to see the towering superyacht docked in the port.

The design stands out from other boats, not just because of its size, but also its dynamic tiered design.



The long lines of the decks emphasise the sleek length of the superlong boat.

It can accommodate 24 guests and a crew of at least 45 people.

Deep Blue boasts all the mod-cons to be expected of a secretive billionaire’s eyewatering superyacht.

A well as an infinity pool and jacuzzi, it also boasts a spa, gym, cinema room and bar.

The interior of the yacht will be flooded with light due to extensive glass windows wrapping around each level of the vessel.



Construction began in 2021, with large pieces affixed in 2023 using a floating dock, according to Superyacht Times.

Known for constructing super long boats, Lürssen is the go-to for the ultra-rich.

It has previously built the Al Said for the Sultan of Oman and Rising Sun for Oracle CEO Sam Ellison.

News.title: Parents of teens killed in 76mph crash say lives have been ‘shattered’…with driver who partied after deaths jailed
News.content:
DEATH SMASH Parents of teens killed in 76mph crash say lives have been ‘shattered’…with driver who partied after deaths jailed

THE heartbroken parents of two teenagers killed in a horror smash – before the driver went out partying and on a skiing trip – have paid tribute.

Harrison Carter, 18, and George Stephenson, 17, died after the Kia Niro they were passengers in crashed into a tree at 76mph.





Speeding driver Madeleine Lonsdale, who had only passed her test 12 weeks before, was jailed last month for two counts of causing death by careless driving.

The 18-year-old partied “repeatedly” and delayed her first court appearance for two weeks to go on a skiing trip after the death crash in Marston, Lincolnshire, the early hours of June 20 last year.

Both boys’ families yesterday released tributes through Lincolnshire Police.

Harrison’s parents, Sarah and David, described their son as “charming, honest and humble”, while George’s mum and dad, Vicki and Bruce, said their boy was “loveable, witty and intelligent”.

Harrison – known as Harry – was a champion golfer and intended to pursue a career in law, having earned a place at Durham University.

George, meanwhile, was an aspiring water polo player and was due to read psychology at the University of Sheffield.

Sarah and David went on to say: “Harry had the most wonderful smile and the biggest heart giving love and time unconditionally to anyone who needed it.



“Harry saw the good in everyone and made a lasting impression on those whose lives he touched.

“Whilst the loss we feel is immeasurable, we also recognise that grief is the price we pay for love.

“Harry leaves a legacy of pure kindness – we could all benefit from being a little more like Harry.”

And Vicki and Bruce added: “Losing George in such a senseless and traumatic way has shattered our family.

“He was the final part of our jigsaw puzzle, and, without him, we can never be complete.



“There is now a numbness in our lives, as we have already experienced the worst thing that could happen to us.

“Waking up each day and remembering that he is gone brings us fresh pain, and the knowledge that we will never hear his voice, see his smile, or be enveloped in one of his wonderful hugs is utterly heartbreaking.”

They described George as “our BFG and he truly leaves a giant-sized hole in all our lives”.

Lincoln Crown Court heard Harry and George were passengers in Lonsdale’s car and were heading to a petrol station to buy snacks, alcohol and vapes at the time of their deaths.

Lonsdale had raced another car at 100mph during the same trip.



Prosecutor Steven Taylor said: “She took a left turn down a rural country road and … down that road for a distance, evidently accelerated to over 70mph.

“In due course she failed to negotiate a right-hand bend further along the road.”

He added: “It appears she misjudged the distance to the first bend and failed to slow down at all on her approach.”

Lonsdale was travelling at 76mph seconds before she collided with the tree – causing the car to land on its side.

The unlit road was subject to a 60mph limit and a sign warned of the upcoming bend.



Harrison, who was in the front passenger seat, and George, who was sitting directly behind him, were both trapped in the car.

Lonsdale, who suffered a fractured wrist, approached a passing driver and asked if he could get the two friends out of the car.

Mr Taylor said: “He saw they were motionless and believed they were already deceased.”

The pair, who would have been rendered unconscious immediately due to their head injuries, were tragically declared dead at the scene.

Lonsdale, who passed a breath test, denied speeding but admitted the bend came up sooner than she was expecting.



Another car driven by a teenage friend was following Lonsdale’s vehicle but managed to avoid the collision, it was said.

Mr Taylor said Lonsdale and the other driver decided to “see how fast their respective vehicles could go” and “effectively raced each other” before the crash – briefly travelling at 100mph on the A1.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

George’s mum Vicki told the court last month when Lonsdale went on a skiing trip, delaying her first court appearance by two weeks, it “only added to the torment”.

Lonsdale was jailed for 14 months and has been banned from driving for three years.

News.title: Hundreds complain of mystery skin condition TSW as doctors baffled
News.content:
Hundreds complain of mystery skin condition TSW as doctors baffled

People suffering from Topical Steroid Withdrawal have spoken up about the devastating combination of severe reactions and the difficulty finding doctors who believe them

View 5 Images Bethany Norman was left screaming with pain from TSW (Image: Bethany Norman / SWNS)

Hundreds of people have sought doctor's advice for a poorly understood but severe skin condition known to wreak havoc on topical steroid users.

‌



Topical Steroid Withdrawal, also known as TSW, is a medication-induced condition whereby users of the anti-inflammatory creams experience a series of severe symptoms. Sudden cessation of corticosteroids, which are used to treat eczema, psoriasis and dermatitis, can bring on itching, burning and redness of the skin.

‌



These symptoms can become so severe - in some cases moreso than the conditions the creams are designed to treat - that sufferers have ended up in hospital.

‌



View 5 Images Bethany's condition left her seeking hospital treatment (Image: Bethany Norman / SWNS)

The BBC reports that hundreds of people suffering from TSW have contacted the broadcaster due to their horror experiences, among them Bethany Norman, 36, who recalls screaming due to the extreme pain in which she was left. She has vowed not to have her baby son take the cream, believing corticosteroids she was prescribed for her life-long eczema had left her with the condition.

She said: "I've been told by countless medics that all I have is a severe flare up of eczema and steroid creams will sort it. They just made it worse."

‌



View 5 Images The mum has said she would never have her son take corticosteroids due to her experience (Image: Bethany Norman / SWNS)

Speaking about her desire to spare her son the same fate, she said: "Look at what this medication has done to me? Why would I put it on my own son?" Another sufferer, Jenna Crosbie, a trainee GP in north Wales, told the broadcaster that doctors are taught corticosteroids are the first line of defence for conditions like eczema.

She remembered seeing a patient with TSW while working in A&E and questioning why they would refuse treatment with the cream when it has proven benefits.

‌



View 5 Images Doctors have described seeing TSW 'like the worst full-body excema' (Image: Bethany Norman / SWNS)

She said: "I remember thinking it looked like the most severe full-body eczema I'd ever seen, and I couldn't understand why the patient was refusing steroids." The trainee doctor, who had used the cream to treat her periodic eczema outbreaks, said she later understood her patient when she saw her own skin change.

Redness that had once been treated had started spreaking, she said, and she decided to stop using the creams, assisted by an understanding GP.

‌



View 5 Images Bethany said she struggled to have doctors believe she was suffering from TSW (Image: Bethany Norman / SWNS)

Bethany, whose condition was more severe, said she had to see up to 30 different doctors, none of whom believed her when she said the creams had stopped working. She said: "I've seen 30 different doctors and not one believed me when I said the creams had stopped working.

"I was being prescribed the strongest potency, I was rubbing it on the affected areas but within minutes the inflammation was back." TSW has been acknowledged as a very real condition, however, and doctors have warned that GPs often go too quickly to corticosteroids.

Article continues below

Dr Dean Eggit, a Doncaster GP, said: "Unfortunately the beginnings of TSW can look like the original eczema rash in the first place. So when it comes to treating those patients, there is a risk we keep prescribing them with the creams that might be causing the condition."

News.title: Fan who survived Hillsborough tragedy when just 13 trying to find stranger who saved his life
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Fan who survived Hillsborough tragedy when just 13 trying to find stranger who saved his life

Fan who survived Hillsborough tragedy when just 13 launches appeal to find stranger who saved his life: Do you know the mystery supporter from Sheffield: email Andy.Lines@mirror.co.uk

Hillsborough survivor searching for the man who saved his life

A football fan who survived the horrors of Hillsborough when he was just 13-years-old has made an emotional appeal to find the man who saved his life that day. Graeme Banfield is making his plea ahead of the 37th anniversary of the tragedy which claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool supporters.

‌



He recalled how a complete stranger - he believes was a Sheffield Wednesday fan - saved him and 16-year-old brother Paul’s lives on the Leppings Lane terrace that Saturday afternoon.

‌



He said simply: “Without this man there would have been 99 dead that day. He saved our lives. I know it’s 37 years on but I’d really like to find him to say ‘thank you’ and buy him a pint.

‌



View 8 Images Liverpool fan Graeme Banfield trying to find stranger who saved his life at Hillsborough (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

“I’d like to say thank you for taking us under your wing and looking after us - even though we were strangers a couple of hours before.” Graeme, 50, has never spoken about his ordeal before. But he went into counselling three years ago and has ended up writing a book. As a 13-year-old schoolboy he was attending his first ever Liverpool away match at the FA Cup semi final between the Reds and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday’s Hillsborough stadium. His worried mum didn’t want her sons to go but reluctantly agreed after seeing their excitement at securing £6 terrace tickets through a family friend. As Graeme was speaking to the Mirror he read through his statement given back in 1989, which still contains gaps and blanks where police shockingly deleted sections.

View 8 Images Graeme Banfield with his brother Paul (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



He said: “Everything in my life started going downhill on April 15th 1989. Hillsborough changed my life for ever. What followed was three decades of grief, self-destruction and resilience.

“I couldn’t talk about what happened for years. But eventually I went into counselling and saw a psychotherapist. He was brilliant and after a year he asked me if I was comfortable writing it down and I agreed. And the result is this book.

”It’s not something I ever thought I would do but I’m very proud of it. My mum died in 1999. I wrote this book for her. It’s in her memory.”

‌



View 8 Images Graeme Banfield plea to find stranger who saved his life (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

Graeme, from Huyton, Liverpool now lives in Douglas, on the Isle of Man, works in retail and was named after his mum’s favourite player Graeme Souness. He has a 16-year-old daughter Amy who is also a Liverpool fan. He explained how he ended up with a mystery fan at the match. He and Paul went with a family friend who had a ticket in another part of a ground. Before the match Liverpool supporters met up for drinks and sandwiches at Sheffield United’s Bramall Lane ground. While they were there they met this mystery fan who also had a ticket for Leppings Lane and kindly offered to take the boys so the friend wouldn’t need to worry. It was a decision that would change their lives for ever affecting all involved. He said: “I’ve always thought about the man who saved my life. There is no doubt he saved my life. He saved our lives.

View 8 Images Graeme Banfield’s South Yorks Police witness statement from Hillsborough. (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



“My memory is he was a Sheffield Wednesday fan but my brother thinks he was a Sheffield United supporter. He was in his early/mid 20s. I would love to find him and buy him a pint to say ‘thank you’ “He’d probably only be in his early 60s now so hopefully he’s still alive and will recognise himself and come forward.” Graeme recalled in detail what happened in that fateful 15 minute period just before the game started until it was abandoned.

He had wanted to watch the game in the middle of the Leppings Lane terrace. They walked through the tunnel but the mystery fan, recognising the potential danger, refused point blank to allow them to stay there. They returned through the tunnel just seconds before the horrific police decision to open the gate.

View 8 Images Graeme Banfield with his daughter. (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



He recalled: “He said: ‘Come on, we're not watching it here.’ I said: ‘What? But we're here. This is where we always watch it, right in the middle behind the goal.’

"No, come with me. I know this ground. I know a better spec." But we're here," I repeated. I didn't want to go anywhere. This was where all the songs would be started and a view right behind the goal. It was perfect But he shouted, ‘No, come on, let's go.’

“I trudged off gutted, but I had to do as I was told because he was looking after us. “We walked back out through the tunnel, turned right around the side, then up these steps.

‌



“There is no way you would have even known there was a section there unless you knew the ground like he did. It was so poorly signposted.” Graeme still has an amazing memory of some of the moments of the day.

View 8 Images TV image of Graeme been passed over a wall by Liverpool supporters at Hillsborough. (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

“There were no stewards anywhere,” he said. "I can still remember two ladies sitting there on chairs at the Leppings Lane end. I think they were supposed to be guiding fans to the right areas. One of them was even knitting.”

‌



He remembered how they reached their safe “vantage point”. He said: “We were higher now. It was really quite empty where we were standing. The match kicked off and we hit the post.

“Then there were some fans shouting at Brucie (Grobbelaar) but he didn't have a clue what was going on. You knew, you could see the desperation and people trying to clamber over the fence, that there was something badly wrong.

“A policeman ran on the pitch to tell the referee to stop the game, and at six minutes past three the game was stopped. There was just a silence in our section of the crowd.

‌



View 8 Images Liverpool fan Graeme Banfield's new book (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

“We were helpless. We just stood in shock as to what was unfolding in front of our eyes.” Later they went outside and met up with the family friend. The local Sheffield man disappeared - never to be seen again. Graeme recalled: “We finally arrived home. We gave Mum the biggest hug. She was so relieved to see us. There were some neighbours knocking to speak to Mum to see if we were ok, and while Mum was talking to them we sat by the fire getting warm. Then to my shock, there I was on the Ten o'clock News - being passed over the fans. It was weird seeing yourself.”

View 8 Images Graeme Banfield plea to find stranger who saved his life (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

Article continues below

Graeme was a pupil at St Margaret’s High School in Aigburth when he went to the game. He recalled: “I went back to school on the Monday and I was crying my eyes out. The teacher said: ‘would you like to miss assembly?’ and that was the extent of my counselling or therapy - in those days that was it.”

He said the counselling he has recently received has transformed his life. He said: “Recently the Hillsborough Survivors Support Alliance have been brilliant. Both Liverpool FC and the Premier League have given them money. This paid for my counselling and a lot of other people’s. It’s great - but it should have happened a lot earlier.”

News.title: Iran war peace talks face major gaps between sides in ending conflict
News.content:
Iran war peace talks face major gaps between sides in ending conflict

Two of the warring parties in the Gulf conflict - the US and Iran - have begun indirect discussions amid a shaky ceasefire, with Israel under pressure over Lebanon attacks

View 6 Images JD Vance arrived in Pakistan to start the talks (Image: PAKISTAN FOREIGN MINISTRY/HANDOUT/EPA/Shutterstock)

Iran peace talks will need to bridge a yawning gap of wants and goals as negotiators come to the table in a bid to make a two-week ceasefire a permanent truce.

‌



Donald Trump officially ceased US operations in the Middle East last week with a pausing of hostilities that drew a messy end to more than a month of bombardments in Iran which critics have argued accomplished very little - if anything at all. Follow-up talks with Pakistan's prime minister began in earnest on Saturday, on a backdrop of deep disagreements and unabated fighting from the US' Israeli warring partners in Lebanon.

‌



Indirect discussions reportedly got under way today between the US and Iran in Islamabad, though it was unclear if the parties were in the same room. A US delegation led by Vice President JD Vance and an Iranian delegation led by Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf must bridge several massive divides.

‌



OPINION Mikey Smith Donald Trump's weirdest week has left him isolated with nowhere to go on Iran

View 6 Images The US entered the war in a desperate bid to prevent Iran from enriching uranium (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Iran's nuclear enrichment

One of the core reasons Trump started hammering Iran was the country's push for continued uranium enrichment, despite claims from the White House in January 2025 that its nuclear facilities had been "obliterated" and suggestions to the contrary were "fake news". When the ceasefire was put in place, Trump proclaimed that Tehran had agreed to hand over its stores of enriched uranium.

‌



The 15-point plan the administration handed Iran demanded the country's regime "end all uranium enrichment on Iranian soil" to fulfill Trump's demand that it "can never have a nuclear weapon".

However, a 10-point plan Trump once praised as a "workable basis" for an overall deal included a demand for international recognition of its rights to continue enriching uranium. The nuclear question may actually end up being less of a sticking point than some of the others, however, as experts have said the assault on Iran has helped Tehran understand it has a new weapon: the Strait of Hormuz.

View 6 Images The Strait of Hormuz is a potent non-nuclear weapon for Iran (Image: Marine Traffic)

‌



The Strait of Hormuz

The most significant fallout from Trump's Iranian adventure is the knock-on effect on fuel prices, with Iran having shuttered the critical Strait of Hormuz shipping artery, forcing commercial vessels to avoid the strait. The closure is Iran's biggest strategic advantage in the war, as it has effectively blocked the passage of oil, natural gas and fertiliser to the west.

The spot price of Brent crude, the international standard for oil prices, was around $97 (£77) on Friday, up more than 30 percent since the war started.

Before the conflict, around a fifth of the world's traded oil typically passed through the strait on more than 100 ships a day, many carrying oil to Asia. With the ceasefire in place, only 12 have been recorded passing through, and Iran has now realised it has a potent non-nuclear weapon against the west.

‌



Speaking to The Guardian, Alan Eyre, a former diplomat who helped negotiate the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which had effectively prevented Iran from making weapons-grade uranium, said it is a "really cool threat".

He said: "The strait of Hormuz is such a good strategic deterrent [and] to an extent it makes the nuclear programme less crucial. It would have taken a lot of time and a lot of risk for them to weaponise [nuclear arms] … But they’ve got a really cool threat now, which is incredibly easy to turn on and off.”

Iran has proposed charging ships passing through the strait as part of a peace deal. But this has been roundly rejected by other countries, including the United States, and Iran's neighbor Oman.

‌



View 6 Images Thousands of people have died in Lebanon during the war in Iran (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Israel's continued assault on Lebanon

When the ceasefire was agreed last week, it was initially believed that Iran was included in the deal and wouldn't be targeted after it came into effect. But Israel continued to fire on the nation, claiming the ceasefire hadn't covered its regional neighbour after its forces killed almost 1,500 people in the nation.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed his forces are solely focused on Hezbollah, a militant group aligned with Iran with which Israel has been warring for decades.

‌



Israel wants the Lebanese government to assume responsibility for disarming Hezbollah, much like was envisaged in a November 2024 ceasefire. But it is unclear whether Lebanon's army can establish a monopoly on arms or confiscate weapons from the militant group, which has survived efforts to curb its strength for decades.

The longer continued targeting of Hezbollah lasts, the more jeopardy the overall ceasefire is placed in. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a statement on X last week: "The continuation of these actions will render negotiations meaningless.

"Our fingers remain on the trigger. Iran will never abandon its Lebanese sisters and brothers." Trump has however failed to put pressure on Netanyahu to fully stop the Israeli action, saying on Truth Social last week that it would be ramped down rather than completely stopped. He wrote on his social media platform that the bombings would be "a little more low key" ahead of the talks.

‌



View 6 Images Israel has continued to hammer Lebanon with the ceasefire in effect (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Iran's 'forward defence'

The war has killed at least 3,000 people in Iran, 1,953 in Lebanon, 23 in Israel and more than a dozen in Gulf Arab states. It has largely cut off the Persian Gulf from the global economy, sending energy prices soaring and damaging infrastructure in half a dozen countries in the region.

Iran has allies across the region that form its "forward defence", which Israel has labelled the "Axis of Evil", including groups labelled terrorist by the country and its western allies.

‌



They have been under near-constant attack since the start of the war in Gaza, and Iran stipulated in its 10-point negotiation document that "all hostilities" would be ceased against its allied groups in the region. Israel and the US' 15-point plan, however, states the exact opposite, stipulating that Iran would stop funding these groups Tehran sees as a critical extension of its own defence.

View 6 Images Iran's regional allies have been hit hard since the October 3 attack on Israel in 2023 (Image: Getty Images)

Sanctions relief

Iran's current Islamic regime has spent most of its life under international sanctions of some kind, but US sanctions were notably lifted in part while Barack Obama's JCPOA was in place. An important US concession under the nuclear deal was limited sanction relief, and, in exchange, Iran permitted monitoring of its nuclear stocks.

Article continues below

Trump pulled the US out of that deal during his first term, claiming it was the "worst deal ever", and the latest Iran operation has brought the country back to square one a decade later.

Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, the speaker of Iran's parliament, said it would only come to the negotiating table if an estimated $120 billion (£89bn) of frozen Iranian was released. He claimed this, alongside the Lebanon ceasefire, was one of two previously agreed measures.

Washington has said it is open to discussing sanctions relief, but officials say this is something they would offer only after receiving concessions from Iran on its nuclear and missile programmes.

News.title: Kemi Badenoch mocked for forces vow after 'hollowing out Britain's defences'
News.content:
Kemi Badenoch mocked for forces vow after 'hollowing out Britain's defences'

Labour Defence Minister Luke Pollard warned Britain would be 'in a war without a plan' under the Tories, over their backing of US/Israeli military action in Iran

View 2 Images Kemi Badenoch was skewered over the Tory record (Image: Getty Images)

Kemi Badenoch has been accused of hypocrisy after the Tories “hollowed out Britain’s defences”.

‌



The Tory leader had called for Britain to show allies like the US a willingness to “get our hands dirty” on defence commitments and undertake “the biggest peacetime programme of rearmament in our country’s history”.

‌



In a speech at the London Defence Conference, Ms Badenoch pledged “the largest net increase in British troops under any government since the Second World War” if they return to power, including recruiting 6,000 regular soldiers and 14,000 reservists.

‌



Trump says Hormuz to reopen 'automatically' and focus of Iran talks is nukes READ MORE :

View 2 Images Minister for Defence Procurement and Industry Luke Pollard mocked the Tory leader (Image: Getty Images)

‌



However, a Labour Defence Minister has now warned Britain would be “in a war without a plan” under the Tories, over their backing of US/ Israeli military action in Iran. Luke Pollard MP said: "Kemi Badenoch’s message is: the Tories hollowed out Britain’s defences, now put us back in charge. Nobody will take that seriously.

“If she were Prime Minister today, Britain would now be in a war without a plan. She wanted to rush in without thinking about the consequences. That tells you everything you need to know about her judgement on defence and foreign policy. And paying for more troops by plunging children into poverty is not a credible plan.

“ Keir Starmer made the right call in ensuring that Britain would not be drawn into offensive action, while supporting our allies in the region. His Labour Government is delivering the biggest sustained uplift in defence spending since the end of the Cold War, with every pound of our defence uplift delivering for British businesses, British workers and British national security.

Article continues below

Ms Badenoch had criticised the PM ”for Britain’s “lack of readiness” after the breakout of war in the Middle East, saying the UK looked “woefully unprepared” while allies like France and Germany mobilised quickly.

Keir Starmer’s Government has pledged to spend 2.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) on core defence by 2027, rising to 3% in the next parliament. Ministers have previously blamed previous Tory administrations for “hollowing out” the armed forces and say they have inherited years of underinvestment.

Real-terms defence spending varied under the Tories between 2010 and 2024, falling by 22% by 2016/17.

News.title: Iran war live: Peace talks start as red lines emerge and Trump says regime 'losing big'
News.content:
Trump claims Iran is 'losing big' with military 'nonexistent'

The US President has taken to Truth Social to slam what he claims is "fake news" related to the war in Iran.

Trump claims Tehran is "losing big" in the conflict, which was sparked by US-Israeli strikes in the joint mission 'Epic Fury' on February 28. While negotations are currently underway in Pakistan amid a fragile 14-day ceasefire, the POTUS claims not only is the US winning the battle, but Iran's military is "largely obliterated".

Taking to his Truth Social platform, he wrote: "The Fake News Media has lost total credibility, not that they had any to begin with. Because of their massive Trump Derangement Syndrome (Sometimes referred to as TDS!), they love saying that Iran is “winning” when, in fact, everyone knows that they are LOSING, and LOSING BIG!

(Image: Getty Images)

"Their Navy is gone, their Air Force is gone, their Anti Aircraft apparatus is nonexistent, Radar is dead, their Missile and Drone Factories have been largely obliterated along with the Missiles and Drones themselves and, most importantly, their longtime “Leaders” are no longer with us, praise be to Allah!", he added in reference to US strikes killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in the early days of the conflict.

However, the Strait of Hormuz, which has essentially cut off a chunk of the world's oil supply since becoming blocked by Iran, remains an issue Trump can't shy away from.

He continued: "The only thing they have going is the threat that a ship may “bunk” into one of their sea mines which, by the way, all 28 of their mine dropper boats are also lying at the bottom of the sea.

"We’re now starting the process of clearing out the Strait of Hormuz as a favor to Countries all over the World, including China, Japan, South Korea, France, Germany, and many others."

In another swipe to nations around the world which have so-far avoided being dragged into the conflict, Trump added: "Incredibly, they don’t have the Courage or Will to do this work themselves.

"Very interestingly, however, empty Oil carrying ships from many Nations are all heading to the United States of America to LOAD UP with Oil."

News.title: TV impressionist Alistair McGowan on mum's death, Huw Edwards rare Judi Dench expletive
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: TV impressionist Alistair McGowan on mum's death, Huw Edwards rare Judi Dench expletive

Now a respected pianist and poet, Alistair McGowan is used to making a big impression as the voice of everyone from Posh and Becks to Sven and Nancy and Dot Cotton

View 6 Images Alistair McGowan as David Beckham alongside Ronni Ancona as Victoria Beckham in Alistair McGowan's Big Impression (Image: BBC)

Thirty years after ITV’s Spitting Image ended its original 12 year run, the man who voiced puppets including Noel Gallagher, Tony Blair, and Peter Mandelson, Alistair McGowan confesses: “I had my fill of politicians on Spitting Image. Politicians were more Rory Bremner’s bag. And I wouldn’t want to sully my mouth having to talk like Trump for any period of time. He’s utterly despicable and against everything I believe in.”

‌



Now 60, Alistair has lost none of his edge, although he is now also a respected pianist and poet, which is reflected in his new tour, Piano, Poetry & Comedy: 3 In 1 - running until October 10. He says: “I’ve always seen myself as an artist more than anything else, so to be able to use these other elements…I love that.”

‌



But he is happy to reminisce about his amazing TV success, especially with the BAFTA winning Alistair McGowan’s Big Impression, which ran on BBC One (later as The Big Impression) from 1999 to 2004, which he starred in with actor, comedian and impressionist Ronni Ancona. It featured hilarious impressions, like those of David and Victoria Beckham, and Sven-Goran Eriksson and Nancy Dell’Olio.

‌



View 6 Images Alistair as Dot Cotton, with Todd Carty as Mark and Adam Woodyatt as Ian Beale (Image: BBC)

Alistair, who also fronted You Cannot Be Serious! on ITV in 2012 and The Week That Wasn’t on Sky One in 2018, says: “The only time I met David Beckham was after he burst on to the scene and I was emerging as someone who ‘did’ footballers. I presented an award to David in 1996 and he said ‘You’ll have to do me soon’ and I remember thinking ‘I doubt I will. One season wonder!’

“I still get people saying they loved the Posh’n’Becks sketch where he gets confused with a chiropractor and choir practice. Nancy Dell’Olio was a distant crush. I thought she was a stunning-looking woman. I met her and Sven in 2003 at a corporate event on a boat going down the Thames. We went past David Blaine in a glass tank suspended above the river. I remember thinking ‘This is surreal. I’m on a boat talking to the current England manager I do an impersonation of and a woman I have a crush on!’”

‌



Born and raised in Evesham, Worcestershire, the young Alistair loved telly shows starring Ronnie Barker and pioneering impressionist Mike Yarwood. He says: “I met Mike on radio and TV projects. In September 2023, Rory Bremner and I were recording tributes to Mike, and as we left we heard that he’d died that day. That was the strangest thing, and the programme got turned into a posthumous tribute.“

6 View 6 Images The Liam Gallagher Spitting Image puppet (Image: Jam Press/Propstore) 6 View 6 Images Alistair McGowan with the Best Comedy Programme or Series award for Alistair Mcgowan's Big Impression he received at the British Academy Television Awards at the London Palladium, Sunday 13 April 2003 (Image: PA)

‌



Alistair speaks fondly of his parents. He was filming the fourth series of The Big Impression when his father Mac, a schoolteacher born in India, died. His mother Marion, whose own talents for playing piano and doing impressions inspired him, died four years ago. He says: “Mum wasn’t well for the last few years of her life, so my whole piano thing passed her by which quite hurt me.

“Yet, she and Dad couldn’t have been more supportive and excited about my success when I was on television. Mum was very proud of that and gave lots of feedback. She just wanted me to do TV all the time. When I released my Piano Album in 2017 [which topped the classical charts] she wasn’t really gushing about it, but she wasn’t herself at that time.”

Also an accomplished actor, Alistair has appeared in two Hollywood movies and numerous TV series and stage shows. He shares a hilarious anecdote about Judi Dench when they appeared together in Merry Wives: The Musical at Stratford Upon Avon in 2006. She drove past someone she thought was him and jokingly shouted ‘w***er!’…only to see it was a stranger.

‌



He says: “She said ‘Al, I can’t believe what’s just happened. I thought it was you and I shouted out w***er! I’m mortified.’ I said ‘well you should be mortified. Just think, there’s some poor bloke wandering around going ‘Judi Dench just called me a wanker for no apparent reason!’ She went ‘oh gosh yes! I hadn’t thought about that, Al.’ Maybe he’ll come out of the woodwork one day.”

View 6 Images Alistair McGowan and Ronni Ancona as The Hamiltons in 2002 (Image: BBC)

In 2008, working on a production of The Mikado, Alistair met singer Charlotte Page, who he married in 2013. He says: “Our wedding was in Ravello, Italy. Just the two of us and some witnesses, no guests. We were back by the pool by midday. We keep saying ‘we must check the certificate to make sure we are actually married in English law.’”

‌



The couple, who have no children but one cat, live in a 5-bedroom 17th Century detached house in Ludlow, Shropshire, where Alistair has held an annual piano festival since 2023 – which this year runs from May 20 to 24. Speaking of his wife in glowing terms, Alistair says: “Very early on I realised that Charlie was very happy for me to be me, which is a particularly nice thing for an impressionist.

“She didn’t know who I was because she didn’t watch television. Not long after we met, she went on a 3 month US tour and watched all my work.” Alistair, who has met King Charles - who he used to include in his act - six times, says the monarch is also an impressionist.

He says: “When he was Prince Of Wales, I used to do a routine in which I had him speaking in a strong Welsh accent. I sat opposite him at a small function in Scotland and he said to others ‘have you seen this routine he does about me being Welsh? It’s terribly funny.’ He told me he did a few impressions and I said ‘you should do the Royal Variety Show. I know a few people and, if you like, I could put a good word in for you!’”

‌



View 6 Images Alistair McGowan and wife Charlotte Page in 2024 (Image: Rupert Barnes Photography)

Recognised less often these days, Alistair says “People over 36 will generally know who I am. Anybody under 36, not a clue! But it’s nice now to walk around or take a train and generally not be noticed.“ Alistair’s newest impressions include Thomas Tuchel, Mikel Arteta, and Kevin Bridges.

But some of his older characters, like Huw Edwards, have been dropped.

‌



He says: "There are issues now with who you can do. There are quite a number of people like that who I’ve had to stop doing for various reasons.

“I do Paddy McGuinness, Monty Don, Raymond Blanc, and quite a lot of old faithfuls. I thought I had retired six years ago when we moved from London to Ludlow. But there are things that crop up. And I have written two scripts which might be filmed within the next two years. That would be a thrill.

“I’m very happily just doing live stuff. Last week I performed to just 30 people in a room in Ted Heath’s former home in Salisbury. It flashed through my mind at one point ‘God, I used to get 6 million viewers on the BBC. Here I am in front of 30 people in Ted Heath’s old house.’ But I loved it. I’ve absolutely no desire to be on television now. I don’t really need to or want to do it.

Article continues below

“Also, the whole social media thing which I avoid completely, would fill me with absolute horror. To get thousands of comments online saying ‘You’re rubbish’ or ‘You shouldn’t have done that’ or ‘You were rude about that person.’ ‘Uggghh, I couldn’t handle that at all. I am at peace.”

*For details of Alistair’s tour go to alistairmcgowan.com and for the Ludlow Piano Festival visit ludlowpianofestival.com

News.title: James Bulger grave vandalism sees man, 78, arrested as ornaments smashed
News.content:
James Bulger grave vandalism sees man, 78, arrested as ornaments smashed

The grave in Fazakerley, Liverpool, was previously damaged in February when the two cherub statues were smashed. It is not known whether the two instances are connected

View 3 Images The grave of murdered toddler James has been attacked twice in a matter of weeks (Image: PA)

A 78-year-old man has been arrested after the grave of James Bulger was vandalised for the second time in just six weeks.

‌



The grave was previously damaged in February when the two cherub statues were smashed. It is not known whether the two instances are connected. James’ mum Denise Fergus told of her “devastation and disgust” after his grave was smashed up again on Friday.

‌



She had just had his resting place repaired and heads of the cherubs replaced after the previous attack, after well-wishers raised over £20,000.

‌



View 3 Images James Bulger's mum Denise Fergus hit out over the vandalism (Image: CHRIS NEILL)

Widow of Brit killed in Canary Island bus crash among 27 hospitalised READ MORE :

James was two years old when he was abducted from a shopping centre in Bootle and murdered by 10-year-old boys Robert Thompson and Jon Venables in 1993.

James' mum Denise said: “It is a relief that someone has been arrested but it continues to be a distressing time for us. I really just want to know why these repeated attacks happened.”

‌



Katie McCreath, Director of KMC Legal & Finance, who is Denise’s legal barrister said: “We can confirm that a 78-year-old man from Kirkby has been arrested in connection with the recent vandalisation of James Bulger’s grave.

"This is an incredibly distressing development for Denise and the wider family, who are once again having to endure the pain of such a deeply upsetting and senseless act.

"The family are understandably devastated. James’ resting place should be a place of peace, reflection and respect. The repeated violation of that space is both shocking and difficult to comprehend.

‌



"We are in contact with the police and will continue to support the family through this process."

After finding the grave had been damaged Denise said: “I am absolutely disgusted that James’ grave has been demolished and devastated again. It has broken our hearts. “The cherubs that we had got repaired with great care just a few weeks ago, have once again had their heads scythed off. How evil do you need to be to vandalise and destroy a child’s grave. I am devastated.”

View 3 Images James' grave had just been repaired when it was vandalised again

‌



After the grave was damaged for a second time Katie McCreath said: “We are deeply saddened and angered to confirm that the headstone of James Bulger has once again been subjected to vandalism.

“This marks the second incident of its kind, and it is both distressing and unacceptable. Denise is understandably devastated. For any parent, a gravesite is a place of reflection, peace, and remembrance. To have that space violated not once, but repeatedly, is something no family should have to endure. The impact of this goes far beyond damage to property. It is a deeply personal and emotional violation.”

A Merseyside Police spokesman said: ‘We have arrested a man from Kirkby after James Bulger's grave was vandalised at Kirkdale Cemetery yesterday, Friday 10 April. At around 1.20pm, officers were informed of damage having been discovered to the grave.

Article continues below

“At 4.10pm, following enquiries, a 78-year-old man from Kirkby was arrested on suspicion of Criminal damage and theft. He has been taken to a police station.”

Temporary Detective Inspector Viki Lanceley said: "A man has now been arrested and we will continue to update and support James’s family as the investigation progresses. I would encourage anyone with information to come forward directly to police as soon as possible, in any of the following ways."

News.title: NHS warning signs of stroke as Eamonn Holmes in hospital after health battle
News.content:
NHS warning signs of stroke as Eamonn Holmes in hospital after health battle

The NHS has the latest list of symptoms and warning signs

View 2 Images The TV star is said to be 'recovering' (Image: Getty )

GB News presenter Eamonn Holmes is recovering in hospital after a stroke, the broadcaster has said. In a statement on Saturday, April 11, a GB News spokesperson said Holmes, 66, "was taken ill last week and it was later confirmed he had suffered a stroke".

‌



They added: "He is currently responding well to treatment. Eamonn has asked for privacy as he focuses on getting better. His colleagues and everyone at GB News wish him a speedy recovery and look forward to welcoming him back to the people’s channel when he is ready to return."

‌



The Northern Irish broadcaster presents GB News Breakfast with his co-host Ellie Costello. Alex Armstrong will present in his absence this week, the broadcaster added.

‌



Holmes has long battled health issues after dislodging discs in his back, which he said previously impinged on his sciatic nerve and affected the mobility of his right leg. He previously spoke about going through spinal surgery, a double hip replacement, and his struggles walking and using a mobility scooter.

Holmes had a couple of falls in May last year, which seemed to have taken place only weeks apart. The former This Morning host was taken to the hospital after a first fall at his home, then fell from his chair live on-air.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



According to the NHS, a stroke occurs when blood stops flowing to a part of your brain. It can affect speech and movement and take a long time to recover. A stroke needs urgent medical help in a hospital because it can be life-threatening. The main symptoms of a stroke can happen suddenly. They may include:

face weakness – one side of your face may droop (fall) and it might be hard to smile

arm weakness – you may not be able to fully lift both arms and keep them there because of weakness or numbness in one arm

speech problems – you may slur your words or sound confused

The easiest way to remember these symptoms is the word FAST. This stands for: face, arms, speech and time to call 999. There are other signs that you or someone else is having a stroke. These include:

‌



weakness or numbness down one side of your body

blurred vision or loss of sight in one or both eyes

finding it difficult to speak or think of words

confusion and memory loss

feeling dizzy or falling over

a severe headache

feeling or being sick (nausea or vomiting)

View 2 Images Holmes has long battled issues after dislodging discs in his back

Symptoms of a stroke can sometimes stop after a short time, so you may think you're OK. Even if this happens, get medical help straight away. A stroke is more likely to happen if you're older, but it can happen at any age.

Article continues below

You should call 999 straight away if y ou think you're having, or have had a stroke or you've had signs of a stroke within the last 24 hours even if they've now stopped. Do not drive yourself to A&E. The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

The cast of Laguna Beach have reunited for the first time since 2006 — and fans are loving it.

MTV’s reality show followed the lives of several high school seniors, including Lauren Conrad and Kristin Cavallari. The first show of its kind, Laguna Beach laid the groundwork for MTV’s wildly popular spin-off series, The Hills.

The special, released Friday on The Roku Channel, reunited Conrad and Cavallari along with their castmates Stephen Colletti, Lo Bosworth, Talan Torriero, Trey Phillips, Christina Shuller, Dieter Schmitz, Jessica Smith, Morgan Smith and Alex Hooser.

Fans were instantly brought back to the mid-2000s from the moments the show’s theme song, “Come Clean” by Hilary Duff, began to play, with one writing on X, “i just got to the credits of the laguna beach reunion and i’m already crying.”

“Watching the Laguna Beach reunion has me so emotional. Life was so different back in 2004,” a fan wrote while another said, “The Laguna Beach reunion is the therapy I didn’t know I needed.”

Lauren Conrad, Stephen Colletti and Kristin Cavallari appearing in New York City ahead of the 'Laguna Beach' reunion ( Getty )

“I didn’t expect to be fully crying multiple times during the Laguna beach reunion,” someone else chimed in as another agreed, “Watching the Laguna Beach Reunion and I’m in shambles. It’s the nostalgia of it all,”

“Watching the Laguna Beach reunion on @TheRokuChannel & why??? am I??? in my feelings?? I wish Team Kristin or Team Lauren was my biggest decision these days,” someone else wrote, referring to the Conrad versus Cavallari feud that permeated not only the show but pop culture throughout the 2000s and 2010s.

“The Laguna Beach reunion special healed something in me. This was eeeeverything to my teenage LB loving heart. What an era it was to be young. So great to see how everyone turned out and doing well,” another fan said.

Hosted by Saturday Night Live alum Casey Wilson, the reunion special looked back on the friendships and highlights of the series, which ran for three seasons from 2004 to 2006. The cast returned for a sit-down conversation to reflect on the series, with scenes filmed at their old haunts interspersed throughout.

Several cast members grew emotional at various points during the reunion, including when reliving their high school graduation. More tears were shed later on during a montage of family-centered moments from the show. There was even a hint of the show’s signature drama, as Conrad and Cavallari sat down together for their first-ever one-on-one on-camera interview.

However, there were plenty of smiles and laughs shared, too.

“This is a serious full-circle moment,” Colletti later said while reflecting on the experience of coming back together 20 years later.

“I can’t imagine doing this without everyone,” Cavallari said. “I’m glad that we’re all still in this together.”

The Reunion: Laguna Beach is available to stream on The Roku Channel.

A 77-year-old British man has died and 27 people were left injured after a tourist bus plunged into a ravine in the Canary Islands on Friday.

Three people are being treated in hospital for serious injuries, including a 73-year-old man and a 42-year-old man, authorities said.

The deceased man has not yet been named, but government officials confirmed on Friday he was a British national.

He was believed to be travelling with his wife, who Spanish authorities said remained in hospital on Friday evening.

open image in gallery Rescuers work at the scene of the bus crash in the Canary Islands (Europa Press Canarias/Europa Press via AP) ( AP )

A state of emergency was declared on the islands after the bus fell from the GM-2 highway near San Sebastian de La Gomera at around 1:15pm. All 28 people on board, including the driver, were taken to hospital.

Investigations are ongoing into the cause of the crash, as police suggested the driver may have been attempting to “fight” a brake failure before the vehicle dropped into the ravine.

Here’s everything we know so far about the crash.

What happened?

Emergency services in La Gomera were first alerted to the crash at 1:15pm on Friday.

Firefighters, police, the Spanish Red Cross and several ambulances, including an air ambulance, were among the emergency responders who attended to the British tourists and driver.

One man was confirmed to have died in the crash, and all 28 people on board, including the driver, were taken to hospital.

open image in gallery One person remains in a serious condition ( Forta )

Three people suffered serious injuries, including a 73-year-old man and a 42-year-old man, who were transported to hospital in Tenerife.

The island is not a mainstream tourist destination but a small and mountainous isle to the west of Tenerife with a population of around 23,000. It has no international airport, and many of the people who spend time there are hikers – especially British and German.

What do we know about the victims?

All 27 passengers on the bus are understood to have been British tourists in the Canary Islands who were reportedly on their way to the San Sebastián de La Gomera dock, where they were due to travel by ferry to Tenerife before flying back to the UK.

While everyone who was on board was initially taken to hospital, all but six people have since been discharged, authorities said.

Of those, one remains in a serious but stable condition, two in a stable condition, and three others are expected to be discharged on Saturday.

The deceased man has not yet been identified. It is understood he was travelling with his wife, who officials said was still in hospital on Friday evening.

Héctor Cabrera, head of emergency operations on the island, told public broadcaster TVE the bus passengers had been "staying at a resort" on La Gomera.

What caused the crash?

The exact cause of the crash is not yet known. But police have said they are investigating whether a brake failure caused the bus to come off the road, after the driver noticed an issue with braking and “tried to⁠ ⁠fight”.

Juan Luis Navarro, the island director of⁠ ⁠the general state administration, told journalists the bus then came off the road and rolled down the slope.

open image in gallery The bus is reported to have stopped before being ‘thrown’ off the road ( 112CANARIAS )

“Fortunately, it stopped before being thrown off the road,” he said. “Otherwise it could have been much more serious.”

Emergency services said the bus is expected to be removed from the ravine on Saturday.

What has the reaction been?

Shortly after the incident, president of the Canary Islands Fernando Clavijo posted on X to express support for the victims and their families.

The British government later confirmed it is supporting the family of the man who died. A foreign office spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British man who died in the bus accident in the Canary Islands and are in contact with the local authorities.”

Foreign secretary Yvette Cooper wrote on X: “My thoughts are with those affected by the tragic incident involving a bus carrying British holidaymakers in the Canary Islands.

“We are in touch with the local authorities & ready to support Brits & their families.”

Teddi Mellencamp has revealed how her new “older” partner has been supporting her amid her cancer diagnosis.

The 44-year-old former Real Housewives of Beverly Hills star — who was diagnosed with melanoma in 2022 and revealed in 2025 that it had progressed to stage four cancer — opened up about the new romance during a recent episode of her podcast, Two Ts In A Pod, with fellow Bravo star Tamara Judge.

Mellencamp said she’s gone on 10 dates with someone, whom she wouldn’t name on the podcast, and is “taking things slow.” As the relationship has developed, Judge asked Mellencamp how her partner deals with her cancer diagnosis.

“He’s pretty good. He’s a relatively, like, positive and logical person in general,” she responded. “He’s older than I am. But the thing that I like the most about him is he makes me laugh.”

Mellencamp said her partner is very considerate of how she physically feels when they’re out, since she’s undergoing immunotherapy. She added that after they recently went to dinner at Craig’s in West Hollywood, he asked her if she wanted to stay out longer, which she felt up for.

open image in gallery Teddi Mellencamp credits her new partner for making her laugh amid her cancer diagnosis ( Getty Images )

“There’s another little place like speak easy or whatever they call it. And he's like, ‘Do you want to go there or are you too tired from your immunotherapy?’” she recalled. “And I was like, ‘I actually have enough energy right now.’ Then I woke up this morning, and I felt like hell.”

She shared that she and her partner are both parents, noting that he has children who recently graduated from high school. Mellencamp has three younger children — Slate, 12, Cruz, 11, and Dove, six — whom she shares with ex Edwin Arroyave.

“This is the part that’s so weird when you’re dating and you’re both parents, like, how are you ever supposed to get past first base?” she asked. “His kids are older, and they live there all the time. My kids are little, and they’re here all the time.”

Mellencamp was diagnosed with melanoma in 2022. Her condition advanced to stage four in 2025 and metastasized to her lungs and brain. She then underwent major brain surgery that removed four tumors.

open image in gallery Teddi Mellencamp said in October that her cancer was ‘all gone,’ but she’s still undergoing immunotherapy ( Getty Images for iHeartRadio )

In October, she told Real Housewives of New Jersey star Dolores Catania on her Two T’s in a Pod podcast that she had “no detectable cancer.”

Mellencamp added that she will remain on immunotherapy treatments for another year. “I’m still going to be having days when I'm feeling sick and stuff because I still am in immunotherapy, so I'm still fighting because you have to be,” she explained.

“I’m not considered in remission or anything like that,” she noted. “The way the [doctors] said it works, it's like one year, then two years, then at three years you're allowed to be considered… in remission.”

Mellencamp previously spoke about dating amid her cancer diagnosis. During an episode of her podcast in July 20225, she hit back at critics who said that she should only be worried about her “kids and staying alive,” not going on dates.

News.title: Arsenal v Bournemouth LIVE: Huge title race twist as Premier League leaders booed off
News.content:
Arsenal missed the chance to open up a 12-point lead over Manchester City ( Adam Davy/PA Wire )

Bournemouth stunned Premier League leaders Arsenal to hand Mikel Arteta’s side a potentially damaging defeat in the title race.

Arsenal failed to add to their nine-point lead and it means Manchester City, who have two games in hand, can cut their advantage when they go to Chelsea tomorrow, before welcoming the Gunners in a title showdown next week.

Bournemouth won at the Emirates last season and were expected to be an awkward opponent, but Andoni Iraola’s side still surprised the league leaders when Junior Kroupi arrived at the back post to volley the visitors into a 17th-minute lead.

It added to Arsenal’s title race nerves but the Gunners were given the chance to equalise from the penalty spot when Bournemouth captain Ryan Christie blocked with a raised arm in the box. Viktor Gyokeres converted with his 18th of the season.

Still, Arteta was not happy with Arsenal’s display as Bournemouth took charge at the start of the second half. Eberechi Eze, Leandro Trossard and the 16-year-old Max Dowman were sent on in a drastic attempt to regain some control.

Bournemouth were still the dominant side and regained the lead when Alex Scott sliced through Arsenal’s defence to finish. A second successive Bournemouth victory at the Emirates also results in a huge swing in the title race.

News.title: Five experts pick their best funds for your ISA in the new 2026 tax year
News.content:
Stock markets are as turbulent as they have ever been. Those not used to seeing their wealth jump and plunge from day to day might well be wary of trying them out for the first time.

But by investing for the longer term, investors who pick a stocks and sharesISA will almost certainly do better than those who play it safe by holding savings in cash – and they will never pay tax on any earnings.

The average stocks and sharesISA account is worth over £65,000, significantly higher than the typical cash ISA, which holds less than £13,500.

“With UK inflation elevated at around 3 per cent over the past year, it’s not a great time to be sitting on cash, especially given that over the past 12 months, the average stocks and sharesISA grew around 11 per cent, compared to an average return of 3.48 per cent for cash ISAs,” explained Dan Moczulski, eToro UK’s managing director.

With the new tax year’s allowance now in effect – worth £20,000 per person – we asked five experts to pick one fund they would be willing to buy into themselves.

While not recommendations for everybody, they offer food for thought, as well as better diversification and lower risk than buying individual company shares.

Scottish Mortgage FTSE 100

Annabel Brodie-Smith, communications director of the Association of Investment Companies (AIC)

Brodie-Smith is going for the Scottish Mortgage FTSE 100 investment trust managed by Baillie Gifford.

This company invests around the world in exciting private companies like SpaceX and Revolut, as well as public-listed companies like Meta, Nvidia and ASML.

They are aiming to invest in the companies shaping the future – a mix of technology, healthcare, consumer services and more. The trust currently trades on a 5 per cent discount and has low charges of 0.31 per cent. This is an investment trust for long-term investors with a high appetite for risk.

This fund went up 27 per cent in the last year and is up 68 per cent over five years.

open image in gallery The Scottish Mortgage FTSE 100 trust invests in global names including SpaceX ( AFP via Getty Images )

iShares Over 15 Years Gilts Index Fund (UK)

Alan Miller, CIO at SCM Direct

This fund tracks the FTSE Actuaries UK Conventional Gilts Over 15 Years Index and is therefore a fund investing solely in sterling-denominated UK government bonds, with a minimum remaining maturity of 15 years. It holds 27 gilts, has net assets of £2.95bn, and carries a Morningstar Gold medal.

There are no performance fees and a charge of just 0.1 per cent a year.

Miller says: “One of the most compelling opportunities in the market is hiding in plain sight: UK government bonds.

“Here’s the number that stops people in their tracks: 4.95 per cent compounded over 10 years is a 62 per cent return before charges, backed entirely by the UK government and sheltered from tax inside an ISA.”

Gilt yields are close to multi-decade highs. Locking in a yield to maturity of nearly 5 per cent inside an ISA wrapper, where all income and gains are tax-free, is exceptional by historical standards, and at an ongoing charge of just 0.1 per cent per annum, virtually nothing is lost to fees.

He adds: “Boring has rarely looked this good. It’s the kind of deal most active fund managers can only dream of offering.”

This fund is basically flat over the last year and up 9 per cent over five years. That’s because interest rates have been very low – as they are now higher, it should fare better from here.

Man Income

Paul Agnell, head of investment research, AJ Bell

Of the Man Income fund, Agnell says: “The fund’s pragmatic and analytical managers, Henry Dixon and Jack Barrat, invest in undervalued UK companies across the market cap spectrum, which are paying a yield at least in line with the market. In order to avoid value traps, the managers also look at a firm’s cashflow and assets.”

So, the team seek out undervalued and unloved companies, of which the UK market continues to present opportunities.

Their investment process centres on identifying two types of stocks: those trading below their replacement cost (what it would cost today to replace a company’s assets and operations) that are also cash generative, and those where the market appears to be undervaluing profit streams.

The fund has made an excellent start to 2026, up over 10 per cent in the first two months alone and was up 28 per cent over 2025. Banks were a key contributor over 2025, led by Lloyds, but with strong contributions also coming from Barclays and Standard Chartered.

The charge on the Man Income fund is 0.9 per cent.

Murray International

Philippa Maffioli, Blyth-Richmond Investment Managers

Murray International aims to blend global diversification with a solid income stream. The yield is around 3.5 per cent.

Maffioli says: “I like Murray International’s focus on dependable cashflows and sensible valuations, rather than chasing the highest yield. It also isn’t tied to the UK market, so you’re spreading risk across regions and currencies.”

open image in gallery Murray International combines global diversification with a solid income stream ( Getty/iStock )

Day-to-day decisions now sit with Martin Connaghan and Samantha Fitzpatrick, but the approach remains consistent: sustainable income with long-term growth potential. If you reinvest the dividends, it can be a strong compounding option over time.

It charges fees of 0.5 per cent. It is up 36 per cent in the last year and up 60 per cent over five years.

Pantheon Infrastructure Plc

Jonathan Moyes, head of investment research, Wealth Club

Pantheon Infrastructure Plc aims to provide investors with some diversification away from global stock markets while providing the potential for attractive equity-like returns over the longer term.

The FTSE 250 trust co-invests alongside some of the world’s leading infrastructure managers. Its portfolio includes large-scale data centres, gas distribution networks, US renewable energy and storage developers, as well as one of Europe’s leading temperature-controlled logistics and transport businesses.

Moyes says: “These assets are prized for their mission-critical nature and long-term contracted revenue streams. Nonetheless, shares in Pantheon Infrastructure change hands at an attractive 13 per cent discount to net asset value.”

That means the shares in the fund are valued more highly than the actual fund, which means easy wins – if that discount narrows. Trusts’ valuations do not always do so, while others might trade at a premium – in other words, more than the sum of their parts.

Investors should note this is a high-risk investment and should form part of a diversified portfolio. The trust has total ongoing charges of 1.29 per cent. The fund is up 30 per cent in the last year, but is too new for a five-year view.

Depending on which investment platform you use, and like any other fund, there may also be share dealing costs, so look to minimise those where you can so they don’t eat into your long-term returns.

When investing, your capital is at risk and you may get back less than invested. Past performance doesn’t guarantee future results.
